Engineering Note: Contract-First Schema Design for Job Payloads

For most of Waypoint's first year, the mobile app's job payload and the backend's database validation drifted apart constantly -- a field would get added to the API without ever being enforced at the database layer, and vice versa. We fixed this by making a single schema the source of truth for both.

The Job Payload Schema is the root JSON Schema document for everything a job payload can contain. It aggregates the Job Core Object Schema, the object schema that defines the required and optional fields every job payload must have -- customer name, address, requested time window, and status. The Job Core Object Schema in turn aggregates two properties we validate strictly: the Job Priority Property, a schema property that constrains priority to one of three known values, and the Job Status Property, a schema property that constrains status to the finite set of states a job can actually be in.

The Job Payload Schema realizes the Job API Schema, the inline API-operation schema that OpenAPI actually serves to mobile clients, so a change to the root schema is automatically reflected in what the API contract promises. Separately, the Address Sub-Schema, a reusable schema definition referenced wherever an address appears, maps to both the Jobs Collection, the database collection that stores every job record, and to that same Job API Schema -- one definition, enforced identically on the way in over the API and on the way it's stored.

Enforcing all of this depends on the Schema Validation Runtime, the system software that actually compiles and runs the JSON Schema validators against every request and every write. The Job Payload Schema satisfies a specific requirement that came out of last year's drift incidents: A Single Schema Change Must Update API and Database Validation Simultaneously. And the Job Core Object Schema realizes the broader goal behind all of this work: Eliminate Payload Drift Between the Mobile App and the Backend.
